sources.claim: A tax credit reduces the tax owed; most credits are nonrefundable and can reduce the tax only to zero, while refundable credits can produce a refund. Eligibility rules apply to each credit.

sections.skill: Explain how deductions and credits differ

questions.prompt: What does a deduction lower?

choices.text: The income that tax is calculated on
The tax itself, dollar for dollar, after it is calculated
The price customers pay for each product
The interest rate on a business loan

questions.correct_answer: The income that tax is calculated on
questions.intro: Two tax words are often confused. A DEDUCTION lowers the income that tax is calculated on (taxable income). A CREDIT lowers the tax itself, dollar for dollar. Example with a made-up 20 percent rate: a 1,000-dollar deduction lowers taxable income by 1,000 and saves about 0.20 x 1,000 = 200 dollars of tax; a 1,000-dollar credit cuts the tax by 1,000 dollars. A credit applies only if the business is eligible, and some credits cannot reduce the tax below zero. Business expenses that are ordinary and necessary for the business are commonly deductible; which credits apply depends on current law, so check with a tax professional.

sections.skill: A coupon on the price versus a coupon on the bill

questions.prompt: A deduction is like which coupon?

choices.text: One that lowers the amount tax is figured on
One that comes straight off the final bill

questions.correct_answer: One that lowers the amount tax is figured on
questions.intro: Imagine two coupons. One lowers the price of the item before tax is added; the other takes money straight off the final bill. A deduction is like the first coupon: it shrinks the amount that tax is figured on. A credit is like the second: it comes straight off what you owe. For the same dollar amount, the second coupon usually saves you more.

questions.prompt: A credit is like which coupon?

choices.text: One straight off the final bill
